title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Seeing them sailing out against them with so few ships, not only the rest of Xerxes's army but also their commanders judged them to be moved by sheer madness, and they too launched their ships, supposing they would easily capture them. Their expectation was reasonable enough, since they saw that the Greeks' ships were few while theirs were many times as numerous and sailed better. With their minds set on this, they came round and enclosed them in the middle. At this, those Ionians who were kindly disposed to the Greeks and were serving in the expedition against their will, counted it a great grief when they saw the Greeks surrounded, feeling sure that not one of them would return home — so weak did they think the power of the Greeks to be. But those to whom what was happening was a source of pleasure were vying with one another, each trying to be the first to capture an Athenian ship and receive gifts from the king — for in their camps the Athenians were talked about more than anyone else.
